title: Delta writes, evolution and table maintenance
summary: What each write does to rows and each maintenance action does to files, history and clients, on one Delta table run locally with open-source Delta.
outcomes: Assign every row of a MERGE to the clause that acts on it and predict omitted keys, scoped snapshot deletes, duplicate refusals and stale replays.
Write a de-duplicated, revision-guarded upsert and a scoped delete-by-source clause, and read their metrics in DESCRIBE HISTORY.
Read the change data feed by version and distinguish schema enforcement, schema evolution and table features by who they affect.
Decide OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, liquid clustering and predictive optimization with their effects on files, reads, compatibility and recovery, separating open-source mechanisms from Databricks-only services.
startingAssumptions: The Delta snapshots module: a version selects files, the folder is not the table, and time travel needs the files to remain.

The versioned-updates policy: newer revisions replace, older never overwrite, equal revisions with different values are conflicts. It is stated here and developed in the ingestion module, which follows this one in the track; its lessons are linked as optional bridges.
Comfort reading short SQL MERGE statements and a few lines of PySpark.
editorialRationale: Write semantics fail in production through silent row loss rather than errors, so the module follows one table through the three MERGE cases, the omitted key, the scoped snapshot delete and the duplicate delivery before touching maintenance. Change feed, schema and table features come next because they change what readers and writers can do. Maintenance ends in a decision table that separates open-source mechanisms from Databricks-only scheduling, and every number is taken from the executed lab rather than argued.

sources.title: Table deletes, updates, and merges
sources.context: Open-source Delta Lake 4.0.0 documentation source, the release the module's lab executes.
sources.caveat: Open-source semantics at one release. Databricks runs its own Delta implementation, and runtime-specific details such as which conditions count toward a duplicate match can differ; check the platform's MERGE reference for the runtime in use.
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: delete removes data from the latest version but not from physical storage until old versions are vacuumed; MERGE supports inserts, updates and deletes; whenMatched clauses may update or delete, whenNotMatched clauses may only insert, and whenNotMatchedBySource clauses may update or delete target rows that no source row matches and cannot reference source columns; clauses of one kind are evaluated in order and all but the last need a condition; a target row that no clause selects is left unchanged; a merge can fail when multiple source rows match and attempt to update the same target row, and the source should be preprocessed to keep one change per key; updateAll and insertAll ignore extra source columns unless automatic schema evolution is enabled; NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is available in the APIs from Delta 2.3 and in SQL from 2.4, and an optional condition is recommended. The delta-spark 4.0.0 jar's own multiple-match error message links to this page.

sources.title: Table batch reads and writes
sources.context: Open-source Delta Lake 4.0.0 documentation source: schema validation, schema updates and data retention.
sources.caveat: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 behaviour; streaming behaviour and platform defaults differ by engine and release.
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: writes are validated against the table schema: every DataFrame column must exist in the table and data types must match, otherwise an exception is raised, and table columns missing from the DataFrame are written as null; columns can be added explicitly with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS or automatically with the mergeSchema write option or the spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled session setting, the write option taking precedence and added columns being appended at the end; overwriteSchema replaces the schema on an overwrite; streams that read a table terminate when its schema is updated; time travel needs both the log and the data files of a version; data files are deleted only by VACUUM; delta.logRetentionDuration defaults to 30 days and delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration to 7 days; log cleanup at checkpoints can leave a version inside the retention window unreadable because every log entry since the previous checkpoint is needed.

sources.title: Optimizations
sources.context: Open-source Delta Lake 4.0.0 documentation source: compaction, Z-ordering, auto compaction and optimized writes.
sources.caveat: Open-source defaults (for example optimized writes disabled) may differ from a managed platform's defaults; check the engine in use before assuming a behaviour.
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: compaction (bin-packing) coalesces small files into larger ones, is idempotent, and makes no data-related change, so a read before and after returns the same results; readers use snapshot isolation and are not interrupted when OPTIMIZE removes files from the log; OPTIMIZE accepts a partition predicate; Z-ordering colocates related values, is not idempotent and re-clusters all files of a partition on every run; auto compaction (Delta 3.1 and above) runs synchronously after a successful write; optimized writes (Delta 3.1 and above) are disabled by default; data-skipping statistics are collected on the leading columns set by delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols.

sources.title: How does Delta Lake manage feature compatibility?
sources.context: Open-source Delta Lake 4.0.0 documentation source for table protocols and table features.
sources.caveat: Feature lists and minimum versions change with releases; compare every client against the table's DESCRIBE DETAIL output before enabling a feature.
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: features are backward compatible, but enabling some breaks forward compatibility, so every workload that references an upgraded table must use a compliant version; a table protocol has a read side and a write side, and a client that does not understand a listed feature cannot read or write the table; CHECK constraints and the change data feed only upgrade the write protocol, while column mapping and deletion vectors also upgrade the read protocol; table features (Delta 2.3.0 and above) are granular flags that succeed protocol versions; the change data feed maps to writer version 4 and reader version 1 in the legacy scheme; protocol version upgrades are irreversible and can break existing readers, writers or both.

sources.title: What are deletion vectors?
sources.context: Open-source Delta Lake 4.0.0 documentation source for deletion vectors.
sources.caveat: Deletion vectors are optional in open-source Delta 4.0.0 and the lab's table does not use them; platform defaults can differ, so read DESCRIBE DETAIL rather than assume.
sources.reviewedEvidence: Page source read in full on 2026-09-23 from raw.githubusercontent.com at tag v4.0.0 of the delta-io/delta repository (the Markdown behind the docs.delta.io page; the rendered site is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and was not fetched). Passages relied on: by default, deleting a single row rewrites the entire Parquet file that contains it; with deletion vectors enabled, some operations mark rows as removed without rewriting the file and readers apply the marks; enabling them upgrades the table protocol, so clients without support cannot read the table; modified data can remain in old files until they are rewritten and vacuumed, and REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites files to purge soft-deleted rows.

claims.description: VACUUM LITE (Delta 3.3 and above) finds removable files from the transaction log instead of listing the directory and fails with DELTA_CANNOT_VACUUM_LITE when the log has been pruned; the default mode lists the directory and also removes files the table never referenced.
claims.context: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 documentation; not executed in lab L05.

claims.description: Log entries older than delta.logRetentionDuration (30 days by default) are cleaned up when checkpoints are written, and time travel needs every log entry since the previous checkpoint, so a version inside the file retention can still become unreadable.
claims.context: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 documentation; not executed in lab L05.

claims.description: Z-ordering re-clusters all files of a partition on every run and is not idempotent, while bin-packing compaction is idempotent and liquid clustering rewrites only data that needs clustering.
claims.context: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 documentation.

claims.description: Updating a Delta table's schema terminates streams that read the table, which must be restarted, and a change-feed read uses the latest table version's schema.
claims.context: Open-source Delta 4.0.0 documentation; streaming is not executed in lab L05.

concepts.definition: One branch of a MERGE statement that acts on a row according to whether it matched: update or delete a matched target row, insert an unmatched source row, or update or delete a target row no source row matched.
concepts.example: Day 2's MERGE updates C (matched), inserts D (not matched) and has no clause for A.

concepts.definition: A delivery that lists only records that changed since the previous one, so a record it omits is unchanged, not retired.
concepts.example: Day 2 lists C and D; A is omitted and must survive the merge.

concepts.definition: A delivery that lists every current record within a stated scope, so a record in that scope that is missing has been retired.
concepts.example: South's snapshot lists only D, so South's E is retired and North is out of scope.

concepts.definition: Delta's refusal of a MERGE in which several source rows match and try to modify the same target row, because the result would be ambiguous.
concepts.example: Two D rows (revisions 2 and 3) match target D, so day 3's naive MERGE commits nothing.

concepts.definition: A WHEN MATCHED clause with a condition, such as s.revision > t.revision, so that only a newer source row replaces the target row.
concepts.example: A's replay with revision 0 is skipped because the table holds revision 1.

concepts.definition: A commit after which a row is no longer selected by the current version, while the files that held it remain in storage until VACUUM removes them after the retention.
concepts.example: Version 6 no longer selects E, yet a read of version 5 still returns it.

concepts.definition: A per-table option that records row-level changes from the commit after it is enabled, readable with change types and commit versions.
concepts.example: Versions 4 to 6 yield seven change rows, ending with E's delete at version 6.

concepts.definition: Delta's refusal of a write whose columns or types do not fit the table's schema, checked before anything commits.
concepts.example: F's append with an unexpected inspector column is refused and no version is added.

concepts.definition: A deliberate change to a table's schema recorded in a commit, such as adding a nullable column, after which older rows read null.
concepts.example: Version 7 adds inspector; A, C and D read null and F reads QA-2.

concepts.definition: A named capability listed in a table's protocol that every client reading or writing the table must understand.
concepts.example: Enabling the change data feed added changeDataFeed and moved the writer version to 7.

concepts.definition: A maintenance command that rewrites many small data files into fewer larger ones in a new version without changing any row.
concepts.example: Version 8 replaces two files with one; its rows equal version 7's rows.

concepts.definition: A command that permanently deletes data files the table no longer references once they have been removed for longer than the retention threshold.
concepts.example: Files replaced minutes ago are not eligible under the seven-day default.

concepts.definition: A table layout declared with clustering keys that OPTIMIZE applies incrementally and that can be changed later without rewriting existing data.
concepts.example: CLUSTER BY (plant) adds the clustering and domainMetadata features to the table.

concepts.definition: A Databricks service for Unity Catalog managed tables that decides when to run maintenance such as OPTIMIZE and VACUUM.
concepts.example: Enabled, disabled or inherited per catalog and schema; absent from open-source Delta.

concepts.definition: A written row per maintenance action stating its effect on files, reads, compatibility and recovery, and who agreed to it.
concepts.example: Weekly VACUUM at the seven-day default, agreed with the table and export owners.

concepts.definition: A VACUUM mode that finds removable files from the transaction log instead of listing the table directory.
concepts.example: VACUUM inspections LITE fails with DELTA_CANNOT_VACUUM_LITE once the needed log is pruned.

concepts.definition: How long a table keeps its transaction log entries before checkpoint cleanup removes them, 30 days by default.
concepts.example: A version whose log entries were cleaned up cannot be time-travelled even without VACUUM.

concepts.definition: A layout technique run by OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY that colocates related values within a partition's files.
concepts.example: Running ZORDER BY (plant) twice rewrites the partition's files twice.

concepts.term: stream restart after a schema change
concepts.definition: The documented behaviour that a stream reading a Delta table stops when the table's schema is updated and must be restarted.
concepts.example: Adding inspector stops the export stream until someone restarts it.

questions.prompt: A MERGE on inspection_id has only WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *. The target holds A and C; the source holds a newer C and a new D. What does the committed version contain?

options.text: A unchanged, C updated and D inserted.
options.rationale: Correct: A is only in the target and no NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause exists, so no clause touches it.

options.text: C updated and D inserted, with A deleted because the source omitted it.
options.rationale: Deleting an unmentioned target row needs a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause, which this statement does not have.

options.text: Only C and D, because a MERGE replaces the target with the source.
options.rationale: That describes an overwrite; a MERGE changes rows only through the clauses it contains.

options.text: Nothing, because A has no source row and the MERGE fails.
options.rationale: A target row without a source row is normal; the failure case is several source rows for one target row.

questions.prompt: The West plant sends a complete snapshot listing W1 and W3. The target holds W1, W2 and W3 (West) and N1 (North). The merge ends with WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.plant = 'West' THEN DELETE. Which rows are deleted?

options.text: W2 only.
options.rationale: Correct: W2 is West and absent from West's complete snapshot; N1 is outside the clause's condition.

options.text: W2 and N1.
options.rationale: N1 is North; the condition limits the delete to the plant the snapshot covers.

options.text: None, because a delete needs a matching source row.
options.rationale: NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE acts precisely on target rows that have no source row.

options.text: W1 and W3, because they matched the snapshot.
options.rationale: Matched rows go to WHEN MATCHED clauses; this delete applies only to unmatched target rows.

questions.prompt: The same day-3 file (D twice at revisions 2 and 3, A at revision 0, a new E) is merged with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT * into a copy of version 3, where D does not exist yet. What happens?

options.text: It commits: both D rows and E are inserted, and A is overwritten by its revision-0 replay.
options.rationale: Correct: no target row is matched twice, so nothing is ambiguous; each unmatched source row is inserted.

options.text: It is refused with the multiple-match error, as it was at version 4.
options.rationale: The error needs two source rows matching one existing target row; D is not in this target yet.

options.text: It commits with a single D row, because Delta de-duplicates inserts.
options.rationale: Delta inserts every unmatched source row; de-duplication is the pipeline's job before the merge.

options.text: It commits but skips A, because revision 0 is older than revision 1.
options.rationale: This statement has no guard, so the matched A row is updated whatever its revision.

questions.prompt: After de-duplication the source holds A rev 0, D rev 3 and E rev 1; the target holds A rev 1, C rev 2 and D rev 1. The MERGE is WHEN MATCHED AND s.revision > t.revision THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *. What are numTargetRowsUpdated and numTargetRowsInserted?

options.text: 1 updated and 1 inserted.
options.rationale: Correct: D passes the guard (3 > 1), A fails it (0 > 1 is false), and E matches nothing, so it is inserted.

options.text: 2 updated and 1 inserted.
options.rationale: A's replay fails the guard, so only D is updated.

options.text: 1 updated and 2 inserted.
options.rationale: A matches the target, so it cannot be inserted; it is simply skipped.

options.text: 3 updated and 0 inserted.
options.rationale: E has no target row to update, and A is skipped by the guard.

questions.prompt: Cinderline deleted lot E at version 6. The change data feed has been on since version 3, the table keeps the seven-day default retention and nobody has run VACUUM. Where can E's values still be read today?

options.text: In version 5 through time travel, and in the version-6 delete record of the change data feed.
options.rationale: Correct: the removed file and the change file both stay in storage until a VACUUM past the retention.

options.text: Nowhere, because DELETE erased E from storage.
options.rationale: A delete only changes what the current version selects; the documentation says storage keeps it until vacuumed.

options.text: Only in version 5; the change data feed never records deleted values.
options.rationale: A delete change row carries the deleted row's values, as the lab's version-6 delete record for E showed.

options.text: Only in the transaction log's JSON, which stores every row.
options.rationale: The log records which files a version uses, not the rows themselves.

questions.prompt: Version 5 of the Cinderline table updated D from 15/3 at revision 1 to 16/4 at revision 3 and inserted E. How many change rows does the feed return for version 5 alone, and of which types?

options.text: Three: D's update_preimage, D's update_postimage and E's insert.
options.rationale: Correct: an update produces a before and an after row, and an insert produces one row.

options.text: Two: D's update_postimage and E's insert.
options.rationale: The feed also records the pre-image, so a consumer can see what the update replaced.

options.text: One row per data file that the merge rewrote.
options.rationale: Change rows are per changed row and change type, not per file.

options.text: Four: an insert and a delete for D, plus E's insert and a delete for the old E.
options.rationale: Updates are labelled update_preimage and update_postimage, and E had no earlier row to delete.

questions.prompt: A nightly MERGE with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT * receives a source that now carries an extra inspector column. No schema evolution setting is on. What happens?

options.text: The MERGE commits and the inspector values are dropped, because UPDATE SET * and INSERT * ignore extra source columns.
options.rationale: Correct: the documentation says extra source columns are ignored unless automatic schema evolution is enabled.

options.text: The MERGE is refused with a schema mismatch, exactly like an append with that column.
options.rationale: That refusal applies to DataFrame writes; a MERGE's star actions ignore extra source columns instead.

options.text: The MERGE adds the inspector column to the table.
options.rationale: Adding a column through MERGE needs automatic schema evolution, which is off here.

options.text: The MERGE writes the inspector values into another column by position.
options.rationale: Star actions match columns by name, so no value is shifted into another column.

questions.prompt: A supplier reads the inspections table with an older open-source Delta reader that supports reader version 1. You enable the change data feed, and DESCRIBE DETAIL then shows minReaderVersion 1 and minWriterVersion 7. What happens to the supplier's reads?

options.text: Nothing changes for them: the change data feed is a writer feature and the reader version stayed at 1.
options.rationale: Correct: only clients that write must understand changeDataFeed; readers are unaffected by a writer-only feature.

options.text: Their reads fail, because every table feature raises the reader version.
options.rationale: Writer features such as the change data feed leave the read protocol unchanged, as the lab's detail output shows.

options.text: They must upgrade, because writer version 7 also applies to readers.
options.rationale: Reader and writer versions are separate requirements; version 7 on the write side binds only writers.

options.text: Their reads now return change rows instead of the table's rows.
options.rationale: Change rows appear only when a reader asks for them with readChangeFeed or table_changes.

questions.prompt: OPTIMIZE has just committed version 8. A long report that started on version 7 is still reading, and a second OPTIMIZE runs immediately. What happens?

options.text: The report finishes on version 7's files, which are still on disk, and the second OPTIMIZE commits nothing.
options.rationale: Correct: readers keep snapshot isolation, replaced files stay until VACUUM, and compaction is idempotent.

options.text: The report fails, because OPTIMIZE deleted version 7's files.
options.rationale: OPTIMIZE only logs the old files as removed; nothing is deleted from storage until VACUUM.

options.text: The second OPTIMIZE rewrites the compacted file again and commits version 9.
options.rationale: With nothing left to compact, a second run adds and removes no files and commits no version.

options.text: The report switches to version 8 mid-query and may count rows twice.
options.rationale: A query reads one snapshot from start to finish; it does not mix versions.

questions.prompt: The table keeps the default seven-day file retention and a job runs VACUUM every night. On day 10 an analyst asks for version 0, whose files were replaced on day 1. What happens?

options.text: The read fails: the replaced files became eligible after day 8 and a nightly VACUUM deleted them, although DESCRIBE HISTORY still lists version 0.
options.rationale: Correct: time travel needs the version's data files, and VACUUM removed them once they passed the retention.

options.text: It reads normally, because the transaction log keeps a copy of every row.
options.rationale: The log records which files a version uses, not the rows; without the files the version cannot be read.

options.text: It reads normally, because VACUUM deletes only log files.
options.rationale: VACUUM deletes data files and never log files, which checkpoint cleanup handles separately.

options.text: Delta rebuilds version 0 from the change data feed.
options.rationale: Change files cover changes after enablement and follow the same retention; they do not rebuild a whole version.

questions.prompt: The inspections table is partitioned by plant, and the team wants liquid clustering on (plant, inspected_on) in open-source Delta 4.0. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Liquid clustering is not compatible with partitioning, so the partitioned table needs a new or rewritten unpartitioned table declared with CLUSTER BY.
options.rationale: Correct: the documentation lists clustering as incompatible with partitioning and ZORDER; ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY applies to unpartitioned tables.

options.text: Add CLUSTER BY and keep the partitions for extra speed.
options.rationale: The two layouts cannot be combined; clustering replaces partitioning rather than stacking on it.

options.text: Run OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (plant, inspected_on) to turn on liquid clustering.
options.rationale: Z-ordering is a separate technique, and it is also incompatible with liquid clustering.

options.text: Liquid clustering exists only on Databricks, so open-source Delta cannot cluster.
options.rationale: Open-source Delta has liquid clustering from 3.1; automatic key selection is the Databricks-only part.

questions.prompt: Predictive optimization is set to ENABLE on the catalog that holds Cinderline's inspections table, a Unity Catalog managed table. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The service may schedule OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for the table, but its retention still decides how far back time travel works, and merge guards and scopes are still yours to write.
options.rationale: Correct: the service automates when maintenance runs; it does not change retention or write semantics.

options.text: Merge guards become unnecessary, because the service de-duplicates source rows before each merge.
options.rationale: The service schedules maintenance commands; it never inspects or repairs the rows a pipeline merges.

options.text: Time travel now works indefinitely, because the service removes the retention limit.
options.rationale: VACUUM still deletes files past the table's retention, whoever schedules it.

options.text: The same setting also covers external tables and open-source Delta engines reading the table.
options.rationale: It applies to Unity Catalog managed tables; open-source Delta has no such scheduler.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague proposes adding WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE to the nightly incremental MERGE so that the table stays tidy. Explain what would happen to lot A on the next quiet night, and what the source would have to send before deleting A is justified.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: On any night when A is not in the incremental file, the unconditional clause would delete A, although nothing said A was retired: an incremental delivery only lists changes. Deleting A is justified by explicit evidence only: a delete record for A from the source's change feed, applied with a matched delete clause, or a complete snapshot of a defined scope that includes A's plant and no longer lists A, applied with a delete clause restricted to that scope.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates what a delivery asserts from what it omits. Naming either an explicit delete record or a scoped complete snapshot as the licence for deletion is acceptable; a row-count threshold alone is not evidence.

selfQuestions.prompt: The South plant will start sending a nullable line column next week. Choose how to evolve the inspections table's schema, say what older rows and older versions will show, and list what you would check downstream before the first delivery arrives.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Add the column deliberately with ALTER TABLE inspections ADD COLUMNS (line STRING) in a reviewed change, or allow it for that one write with the mergeSchema option; avoid the session-wide autoMerge setting, which would evolve every later write in the job. Existing rows read null for line and older versions keep their five-column schema under time travel. Before the delivery: tell the owners of streams reading the table, because a schema change stops them until restarted; check views, exports and dashboards that list columns explicitly; and confirm every client supports the table's protocol.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer prefers the narrowest switch, predicts null for old rows and the old schema for old versions, and names downstream readers. Choosing ALTER TABLE or a single mergeSchema write are both acceptable, as is withSchemaEvolution() on one MERGE when the column arrives through a merge; a blanket session setting is not.

selfQuestions.prompt: A storage review proposes a weekly VACUUM on the shared inspections table, which a quality dashboard and a supplier export stream read. Write the decision row: its effect on files, reads, compatibility and recovery, who must agree, and the evidence you need before it runs.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Files: each run deletes data files, including change files, that were removed longer than the retention ago. Reads: the current version is unchanged, but time travel beyond the retention stops working and a consumer that lags longer loses changes. Compatibility: unchanged, no feature is added. Recovery: history shrinks to the retention window. Agreement: the table owner, the dashboard owner and the export stream owner. Evidence first: the longest reader and stream lag, the history the business needs, a DRY RUN listing, and confirmation that the retention check stays on at the default or longer.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The row covers all four effects, names the consumers who bear the risk, and grounds the schedule in measured lag and a dry run. Adding a raised retention to protect the export stream is an acceptable variant; a shorter one is not.

beats.title: A MERGE sorts every row into one of three cases
beats.outcome: Assign each source and target row of a small MERGE to the clause that acts on it, or to no clause at all.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-writes-merge-concept|MERGE]] joins a source to a target on its key, then sorts every row into one of three cases. A source row that matches a target row goes to WHEN MATCHED, which can update or delete. A source row that matches nothing goes to WHEN NOT MATCHED, which can only insert. A target row that no source row matches goes to WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, but only if you wrote that clause. Notice in the second table that A, present only in the target, falls to the third case, and nothing happens to it.

handbook.markdown:
Cinderline's day-2 merge in SQL, as the lab runs it against a path-addressed table:

```sql
MERGE INTO delta.`/tmp/lab/inspections` AS t
USING incoming AS s
ON t.inspection_id = s.inspection_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
```

**Where versions 0 to 3 came from.** The lab starts from the snapshots module's numbers in its own commits: version 0 wrote A (10 inspected), version 1 appended C (8), version 2 corrected A to 12 with an in-place UPDATE, and version 3 enabled the change data feed. That UPDATE left A's revision at 1, which is why A reads 12 inspected at revision 1 here while the snapshots and ingestion modules call the same correction A revision 2. It is a data fix, not how a source correction should arrive: a correction is a new, higher revision, and this module's guard trusts only revisions that grow.

The open-source Delta 4.0.0 documentation states the clause rules precisely. There can be any number of WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses. A matched clause may update or delete; a not-matched clause may only insert; a not-matched-by-source clause may update or delete a target row and cannot read source columns, because there is no source row. Clauses of one kind are evaluated in order, and every one except the last needs a condition. A row that no clause selects keeps its values. `UPDATE SET *` and `INSERT *` expect the source to carry every target column.

**What to inspect.** `DESCRIBE HISTORY` records each MERGE with `operationMetrics` and `operationParameters`. In the lab, version 4 reported `numSourceRows=2`, `numTargetRowsUpdated=1`, `numTargetRowsInserted=1`, `numTargetRowsDeleted=0`, and its parameters listed one matched predicate (update), one not-matched predicate (insert) and an empty `notMatchedBySourcePredicates`. Reading those parameters is the fastest way to confirm what a production merge was allowed to do.

**Worked prediction.** Target A, C; source C, D. Case table: A target only, C both, D source only. Clauses written: matched and not matched. Result: A unchanged, C updated, D inserted, three rows. Change the source to C only and the result is two rows with C updated.

**Limits.** WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is available in the open-source APIs from Delta 2.3 and in SQL from 2.4. Databricks follows the same clause model but documents runtime-specific details; check the MERGE reference for the runtime in use rather than assuming open-source behaviour.

beats.recap: Matched rows can update or delete, unmatched source rows can only insert, and target-only rows change only if a NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause exists.

beats.title: Silence in an incremental delivery is not a delete
beats.outcome: Explain why a key missing from an incremental delivery must survive the merge, and name the deliveries that could retire it.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-delta-writes-incremental-concept|incremental delivery]] lists what changed since the last one. Cinderline's day-2 file lists C's new revision and a new lot D; A is simply not mentioned. The delivery asserts nothing about A, so the correct merge has no clause that touches it. Notice in the second state that A is still selected at version 4 with its earlier values. The third state shows the wrong reading: a delete for unmentioned rows would remove A on every quiet night.

samajh.text: Socho society ka dhobi har Monday sirf wahi kapde laata hai jo is hafte dhule. Aapki neeli shirt is baar bundle mein nahi hai, toh kya use almari se nikaal ke phenk doge? Bilkul nahi: bundle sirf batata hai ki kya badla, poori almari ki list nahi hai. Kaun si cheez sach mein gayi, yeh tab pata chalega jab koi poori almari ginke list de.
samajh.mapping: The dhobi's weekly bundle is an incremental delivery, the almirah is the target table, and a full almirah count is a complete snapshot.
samajh.boundary: A real feed may also carry explicit delete records, which are instructions rather than silence; the analogy covers only what absence means.

handbook.markdown:
Three delivery shapes need three different merges, and confusing them is the most common way an upsert destroys valid rows.

| Delivery | What absence means | Delete evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental changes | nothing: the row did not change | none |
| Change feed with operations | nothing | an explicit delete record |
| Complete snapshot of a scope | retired, inside the scope only | the row's absence |

For an incremental file the merge has two clauses, matched and not matched, and no NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause. For a change feed that carries an operation column, a delete is an instruction, not a silence:

```sql
MERGE INTO inspections AS t USING changes AS s
ON t.inspection_id = s.inspection_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'DELETE' THEN INSERT *
```

Only a complete snapshot makes absence meaningful, and only for the population it covers; the next beat scopes that clause.

**Evidence from the lab.** Version 4 kept A at 12 inspected and revision 1 while C and D changed, and its history entry shows an empty list of not-matched-by-source predicates. **What to ask the source owner.** Is this file changes-only, a change feed with operations, or a complete snapshot, and of which scope? Is the answer written in the delivery contract? The ingestion module treats that contract in depth; here the point is that the merge must encode it. **Failure to watch for.** A partial or truncated snapshot looks like a complete one; guard a snapshot merge with a row-count or manifest check before any delete clause runs.

beats.recap: An incremental file says what changed; its silence about a row is never a reason to delete it.

beats.title: A complete snapshot retires rows only inside what it covers
beats.outcome: Scope a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE delete to the population a complete snapshot describes, and predict the damage of an unscoped one.
beats.explanation: South sends a [[dbxfe-delta-writes-snapshot-concept|complete snapshot]] of its open lots, and it lists only D. Now absence means retired, but only for South. The clause WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.plant = 'South' THEN DELETE removes E and leaves North alone. Notice in the second table that dropping the plant condition also deletes A and C, rows the delivery never described. The condition carries the snapshot's scope, because the clause itself cannot know it.

handbook.markdown:
The scoped statement from the lab:

```sql
MERGE INTO delta.`/tmp/lab/inspections` AS t
USING snapshot AS s
ON t.inspection_id = s.inspection_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.revision > t.revision THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.plant = 'South' THEN DELETE
```

Delta evaluated four target rows. D matched but was not newer (3 > 3 is false), so it was unchanged. E is South and absent, so it was deleted. A and C are absent too, but the condition excludes North. Version 6 reported `numTargetRowsDeleted=1` and `numTargetRowsNotMatchedBySourceDeleted=1`.

The same statement without `AND t.plant = 'South'`, run only against a disposable copy of version 5, reported three deletions and left D alone in the table. The Delta documentation recommends an optional condition on this clause to avoid rewriting the whole target; here the condition is also what makes the result correct.

**Designing the scope.** Write the scope from the delivery contract: a plant, a source system, a business date, or a partition of keys. If the snapshot is dated, restrict the delete to rows of that date's population. **Protect against partial files.** Before merging a snapshot, compare its row count or manifest with the expected size and refuse a file that shrank sharply; a truncated snapshot would otherwise retire valid rows. **Inspect afterwards.** Read the deletion metrics in DESCRIBE HISTORY and, when the change data feed is on, the delete rows it recorded.

beats.recap: A snapshot's silence retires rows only inside the scope written into the delete clause's condition.

beats.title: Two source rows updating one target row stop the whole MERGE
beats.outcome: Predict when Delta refuses a MERGE for duplicate matches, and state what the table looks like afterwards.
beats.explanation: Day 3 carries two rows for D, revisions 2 and 3, and D already exists in the target. Both source rows match one target row, so the update is ambiguous: which revision should win? Delta refuses the whole statement with a [[dbxfe-delta-writes-duplicate-concept|multiple-match error]] instead of guessing. Notice in the second state that nothing is half-applied: E is not inserted and the table stays at version 4. The error protects matched keys; it is not a de-duplication step.

Lekin agar naya kurta hai jiska pehle koi naap hi nahi tha, aur do parchiyaan aa gayin, toh jaldbaaz darzi do kurte hi sil dega.

samajh.boundary: Delta never asks anyone which row is final; it refuses the statement, and it inserts duplicate new keys without warning, so choosing the winner is always your code's job.

handbook.markdown:
The refusal as open-source Delta 4.0.0 printed it in the lab:

```text
[DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched and
attempted to modify the same target row in the Delta table in possibly conflicting ways.
```

The documentation's reasoning is SQL semantics: when several source rows match one target row, it is unclear which source row should update it, so the operation fails and the source should be preprocessed to one change per key. DESCRIBE HISTORY still ended at version 4 and a read returned the same three rows.

**The trap on first arrival.** The same day-3 file, merged into a copy of version 3 where D did not exist yet, was *not* refused. No target row was matched twice, so Delta inserted both D rows, inserted E and let A's stale revision-0 replay overwrite revision 1: five rows, two of them D. The multiple-match error guards matched keys only, which is why de-duplication belongs before every merge, not only after an error.

**Runtime differences.** Databricks documents that which conditions count toward a duplicate match differs between Databricks Runtime 16.0 and above and 15.4 LTS and below, so do not rely on a clause condition to dodge the error without checking the runtime. **What to inspect.** Count source rows per key before merging (`GROUP BY inspection_id HAVING count(*) > 1`) and log the offenders; a refused merge commits nothing, so the fix is upstream of the statement.

beats.recap: Two source rows updating one matched target row make Delta refuse the whole MERGE; duplicates of a new key slip in.
beats.changeNote: Narrowed the title and recap: Delta refuses a MERGE when two source rows try to update one target row, not whenever two rows match; a MERGE whose only matched action is an unconditional DELETE is not refused (Delta's MERGE source code, MergeIntoCommandBase.scala, at the v4.0.0 tag).

beats.title: De-duplicate first, then let only a newer revision win
beats.outcome: Write a guarded upsert that keeps one source row per key and refuses stale replays, and predict its metrics.
beats.explanation: The fix has two halves. First keep one source row per key, the highest revision, so D arrives once as revision 3. Then add a [[dbxfe-delta-writes-guard-concept|guarded update]]: WHEN MATCHED AND s.revision > t.revision. Notice in the second table that the guard also blocks A's replay: revision 0 is older than the table's revision 1, so the 99 inspected never lands. E matches nothing and is inserted. Delta reported one update, one insert and three source rows for version 5.

samajh.boundary: The guard trusts whatever revision column you name; a wrong or reset revision wins or loses silently, which a shopkeeper might notice and Delta never will.

handbook.markdown:
The lab's two halves in PySpark:

```python
from pyspark.sql import Window, functions as F
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

latest = Window.partitionBy("inspection_id").orderBy(F.col("revision").desc())
deduped = (day3.withColumn("_rank", F.row_number().over(latest))
               .filter("_rank = 1").drop("_rank"))

(DeltaTable.forPath(spark, table).alias("t")
    .merge(deduped.alias("s"), "t.inspection_id = s.inspection_id")
    .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.revision > t.revision")
    .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
    .execute())
```

Version 5 reported `numSourceRows=3`, `numTargetRowsUpdated=1`, `numTargetRowsInserted=1`, and the history entry recorded the guard as the matched predicate. A stayed at 12 inspected, revision 1.

**Make the de-duplication deterministic.** `row_number()` over a tie picks an arbitrary row. If two source rows share a key and a revision but differ in values, that is a conflict, not a duplicate: route it to review instead of letting the window choose. The versioned-updates lesson of the ingestion module, which comes after this module in the track and is an optional bridge here, sets the policy (newer replaces, identical equal revision is a no-op, older cannot overwrite, equal revision with different values is a conflict); this beat is how the merge enforces it.

**The guard needs a trustworthy revision.** It compares only the column you name. A source that resets revisions, or sends timestamps from unsynchronised clocks, defeats it silently. **Test it on purpose.** Include a stale replay in the test data, as the lab does with A revision 0, and assert that the table did not move.

beats.recap: One row per key before the merge, and a revision guard in the matched clause, keep stale replays out.

beats.title: A DELETE commits a new version; the old bytes stay
beats.outcome: Explain what a DELETE or UPDATE changes in the log and on disk, and when the removed rows physically disappear.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-writes-delete-concept|logical delete]], by DELETE or by a MERGE delete clause, commits a new version that no longer selects the row. Without deletion vectors, Delta rewrites each file holding a deleted row and logs the old file as removed; the old file stays on disk. Notice in the timeline that E disappears from version 6 while a read of version 5 still returns it. The bytes leave storage only when VACUUM runs after the retention, so a delete is not yet an erasure.

handbook.markdown:
The file mechanics are the same for DELETE, UPDATE and the MERGE clauses that change rows. The open-source documentation's default: deleting even one row rewrites the entire Parquet file that contains it (copy-on-write), and the log records an add action for the new file and a remove action for the old one. In the lab the UPDATE of A reported `numUpdatedRows=1`, `numCopiedRows=0`, `numRemovedFiles=1`, `numAddedFiles=1`: A sat alone in its file, so nothing else had to be copied. A file holding a thousand rows would have copied 999 of them.

**Deletion vectors** change the physics, not the meaning. With them enabled, some operations mark rows as removed without rewriting the file, and readers apply the marks; the bytes then leave only after a rewrite (OPTIMIZE, or `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`) and a VACUUM past the retention. Enabling them upgrades the protocol, so check every reader first; read `DESCRIBE DETAIL` rather than assuming a table's setting.

**Where a deleted row can still be read, until VACUUM:** older versions through time travel; change files under `_change_data`, whose delete record carries the row's values when the change data feed is on; and any copy downstream, which Delta does not track at all.

**Erasure is a process, not a statement.** When a legal or contractual erasure applies, the table owner and the responsible legal or privacy function decide the steps and their timing: the delete, purging soft-deleted rows if deletion vectors are used, a VACUUM at the agreed retention, and the downstream copies. This module does not prescribe that process, and it never shortens a shared table's retention or disables its safety check to speed an erasure.

beats.recap: A delete changes what the current version selects; storage forgets the row only after VACUUM passes the retention.

beats.title: The change data feed records from the commit after you enable it
beats.outcome: Read change rows by version, tell pre-images from post-images, and predict when a change-feed read is refused.
beats.explanation: The [[dbxfe-delta-writes-feed-concept|change data feed]] is off by default. Setting delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true is itself a commit, version 3 here, and records nothing retroactively. From version 4 on, every change is readable as a row with a _change_type of insert, update_preimage, update_postimage or delete, plus its _commit_version. Notice in the third table that a range starting at version 2 is refused. Change files follow the table's retention, so VACUUM removes old ones.

handbook.markdown:
Enable, then read a version range (both ends inclusive):

```sql
ALTER TABLE inspections SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);
SELECT * FROM table_changes('inspections', 4, 6);
```

```python
(spark.read.format("delta").option("readChangeFeed", "true")
     .option("startingVersion", 4).option("endingVersion", 6).load(path))
```

The lab read seven rows: C's pre-image (8/0, revision 1) and post-image (8/1, revision 2) and D's insert at version 4; D's pre- and post-image and E's insert at version 5; E's delete at version 6. A consumer applying changes uses the post-image and the delete; an auditor compares pre- and post-image; nobody sums both.

**Storage and cost.** UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE commits write change files under `_change_data`; insert-only commits can be computed from the log instead. The documentation describes the overhead as not significant, and change files follow the table's retention, so a VACUUM past it deletes them and consumers that lag longer lose changes.

**Protocol.** Enabling the feed is a writer-side feature: in the lab `DESCRIBE DETAIL` moved from writer version 2 to 7 with `changeDataFeed` listed while readers stayed at version 1. The feed's page says writers on Delta 1.2.1 or older can no longer write, but the break is wider here: a writer must support table features (writer version 7, from Delta 2.3.0 in the compatibility table) as well as changeDataFeed, so writers on Delta 2.0 to 2.2, which know the feed itself, cannot write either.

**Refusal.** `DELTA_MISSING_CHANGE_DATA` names the first version without change data and suggests `DESCRIBE HISTORY` to find the enabling commit. **On Databricks** the current page also describes an automatic change data feed for eligible Unity Catalog tables on recent runtimes, distinct from this property; check which mode a table uses before designing a consumer.

beats.recap: The feed starts at the commit that enables it, labels every change, and expires with the table's retention.

beats.title: An unexpected column is refused before anything commits
beats.outcome: Predict which writes schema enforcement refuses and which it accepts, including how a MERGE treats extra columns.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-writes-enforcement-concept|Schema enforcement]] checks each write against the table's schema. F arrives with an inspector column the table lacks, so the append is refused with 'A schema mismatch detected' and no version is committed. Notice in the second table that a missing column is treated differently: a table column absent from the batch is written as null. A MERGE with UPDATE SET * differs again: extra source columns are ignored unless automatic evolution is on.
beats.recap: An extra column refuses an append, a missing nullable column writes null, and UPDATE SET * ignores extras.

beats.title: Schema evolution is a commit you choose, one write at a time
beats.outcome: Choose between an explicit ALTER, a per-write mergeSchema option and a session-wide setting, and predict what old rows and old versions show.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-writes-evolution-concept|Schema evolution]] adds the new column inside a commit. With .option("mergeSchema", "true") on one append, version 7 gains a nullable inspector column: A, C and D read null, F reads QA-2. Notice in the first two tables that reading version 6 still returns five columns, because each version keeps its own schema. Prefer the narrowest switch: an explicit ALTER TABLE or one write's or one MERGE's option, not a session-wide setting that silently evolves every later write.

Lekin agar principal keh de ki 'jo bhi naya khaana kisi form pe dikhe, seedha school ki file mein jod do', toh kisi bachche ki galti se likha 'bllod grp' bhi hamesha ke liye naya khaana ban jaayega.

samajh.boundary: Delta also keeps each version's schema, so time travel shows the old form layout; paper files have no such history, and evolution here only adds columns, never renames or drops them.

handbook.markdown:
Four switches add a column, from narrowest to widest:

```sql
ALTER TABLE inspections ADD COLUMNS (inspector STRING);   -- explicit, reviewed, one commit
```

```python
batch.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save(path)   # this write only
(DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t").merge(src.alias("s"), "t.inspection_id = s.inspection_id")
    .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
    .withSchemaEvolution().execute())                                                  # this MERGE only (Delta 3.2+)
spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled", "true")                   # every write after it
```

The documentation says the write option takes precedence over the session setting and that added columns are appended at the end of the schema. Its 4.0.0 merge page still says a MERGE evolves the schema only when the session setting is on, but the merge builder has had `withSchemaEvolution()` since Delta 3.2, scoped to that one MERGE. Run locally on Spark 4.0.4 with delta-spark 4.0.0 and autoMerge unset, it added inspector, and the same MERGE without it ignored the column. The SQL form `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO` parsed and merged the rows in that run but added no column, so check the column list after any evolving MERGE. `overwriteSchema` is a different, heavier tool: it replaces the schema and partitioning during an overwrite.

**Observed in the lab.** Version 7's columns were the five originals plus `inspector`; version 6 read by `versionAsOf` returned five columns; A, C and D read null because their files never had the column.

**Downstream effects to plan.** The documentation states that streams reading a table terminate when its schema is updated and must be restarted. Views that select explicit columns keep their old shape until recreated. A consumer of the change data feed sees the latest version's schema. Renames and drops are not additive: without rewriting data files they need column mapping, a reader-and-writer feature with its own compatibility cost; otherwise the table is rewritten with `overwriteSchema`.

**Why not the session switch.** With autoMerge on, a misspelt column in any later batch becomes a permanent column, and nobody reviewed it. Evolution should leave a trace a reviewer can find: a DDL statement or one write with an explicit option.

beats.recap: Evolve with an explicit ALTER or one write's mergeSchema option; old rows read null and old versions keep their schema.
beats.changeNote: Corrected the note on renaming and dropping columns: column mapping is needed only to do it without rewriting data files; otherwise the table can be rewritten with overwriteSchema (Delta Lake's batch reads and writes documentation, delta-batch.md, at the v4.0.0 tag).

beats.title: A table feature binds every writer, and some bind readers too
beats.outcome: Name the table features this module's actions add, say whether readers or only writers must support them, and check clients before enabling one.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delta-writes-feature-concept|table feature]] is a flag in the table's protocol that clients must understand. In the lab, enabling the change data feed added changeDataFeed and raised the writer version from 2 to 7 while readers stayed at version 1. Declaring liquid clustering added clustering and domainMetadata. Notice in the matrix which actions touch only the write protocol and which also bind readers. A protocol upgrade cannot simply be undone, so list every reader and writer first.

handbook.markdown:
`DESCRIBE DETAIL` shows the protocol in three fields: `minReaderVersion`, `minWriterVersion` and `tableFeatures`. The lab read them three times:

| Table state | Reader | Writer | Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| version 2 | 1 | 2 | appendOnly, invariants |
| version 3, feed enabled | 1 | 7 | appendOnly, changeDataFeed, invariants |
| clustered table | 1 | 7 | appendOnly, clustering, domainMetadata, invariants |

Writer version 7 means the write protocol lists named features instead of implying them from a version number, so a writer needs table-feature support (Delta 2.3.0 or later in open source) before it can write at all; reader version 3 does the same for reads. The open-source documentation classifies the change data feed and CHECK constraints as write-protocol features, while column mapping and deletion vectors also upgrade the read protocol, so they can lock out old readers.

**Before enabling a feature on a shared table**, list every client that reads or writes it (Spark jobs, streaming consumers, BI connectors, other engines, partner readers), record the Delta version or protocol support of each, and compare that list with the feature's side. The retained Delta module's protocol beat gives the general check; this module adds the concrete features its own actions bring.

**Reversal is limited.** The versioning page calls protocol upgrades irreversible, yet from Delta 3.0.0, so in 4.0.0 too, `ALTER TABLE ... DROP FEATURE` can remove some features and downgrade the protocol (in 4.0.0 deletionVectors, columnMapping, checkConstraints and a few others). The 4.0.0 page and the 4.0.0 code differ on how it runs. The page describes two runs at least 24 hours apart, the second with `TRUNCATE HISTORY`, which removes older table history. The 4.0.0 code by default drops the feature in one run, without that wait or `TRUNCATE HISTORY`, and it refuses `TRUNCATE HISTORY` when dropping checkConstraints. Try the drop on a copy of the table before relying on it. The features this module enables, changeDataFeed, clustering and domainMetadata, cannot be dropped in 4.0.0. On Databricks, the feature compatibility page lists which runtime supports each feature.

beats.recap: Every feature you enable binds every writer, and reader features bind every reader too; check clients first.
beats.changeNote: Corrected the section on undoing a table feature: Delta Lake 4.0.0 can drop some features, but not changeDataFeed, clustering or domainMetadata (Delta's drop-feature documentation at the v4.0.0 tag). It also now says the 4.0.0 code drops a feature in one run by default, not in the two-stage wait that page describes (Delta's DROP FEATURE source code at the v4.0.0 tag).

beats.title: OPTIMIZE rewrites files and leaves every row alone
beats.outcome: Trace one compaction through the files, the log and a concurrent read, and predict what a second run does.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-writes-optimize-concept|OPTIMIZE]] bin-packs small files into fewer larger ones in a new version. In the lab, version 8 removed the current version's two files and added one, and version 8 selects exactly version 7's rows. Notice in the timeline that the two old files stay on disk: a reader of version 7 keeps working under snapshot isolation and time travel still finds them. A second OPTIMIZE had nothing to compact, reported zero files and committed no version.

handbook.markdown:
```sql
OPTIMIZE inspections;                                     -- bin-packing compaction
-- only on a table partitioned by inspected_on: WHERE accepts partition columns only
OPTIMIZE inspections WHERE inspected_on >= '2026-09-01';
-- plant must be a data column, not a partition column; Z-ordering is not idempotent
OPTIMIZE inspections ZORDER BY (plant);
```

No single table runs all three lines. On Delta 4.0.0 a WHERE on a data column is refused with DELTA_NON_PARTITION_COLUMN_REFERENCE, and ZORDER BY a partition column with DELTA_ZORDERING_ON_PARTITION_COLUMN; the lab's table is unpartitioned and ran only the first line.

The lab's numbers: the first run returned `numFilesRemoved=2`, `numFilesAdded=1`; `DESCRIBE DETAIL` then showed one file; the folder held eight Parquet data files instead of seven, because nothing was physically deleted. The second run returned zero and zero and the history still ended at version 8, matching the documentation's statement that bin-packing is idempotent.

**Why it is safe to run beside readers.** The documentation states that readers use snapshot isolation and are not interrupted when OPTIMIZE removes files from the log, that a read before and after returns the same results, and that a table used as a streaming source is not affected. Concurrent writers are a different question: OPTIMIZE can conflict with a DELETE, UPDATE or MERGE that rewrites the same files, which the retained module's concurrency beat explains.

**Costs to plan.** Storage grows until VACUUM removes the replaced files. Z-ordering rewrites all files of a partition on every run, and liquid clustering replaces it for new tables. Open-source Delta 3.1 and above also offers auto compaction after writes and optimized writes (disabled by default); a managed platform may run compaction for you. **What to inspect.** The OPTIMIZE metrics in DESCRIBE HISTORY and the file count in DESCRIBE DETAIL, before and after, and whether queries actually read fewer files.

beats.recap: Compaction changes which files a version selects, never its rows, and a repeat run with nothing to do commits nothing.

beats.title: VACUUM trades recoverable history for storage, so retention is a promise
beats.outcome: Decide when a removed file becomes eligible for VACUUM, and explain why the retention check exists and stays on.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-writes-vacuum-concept|VACUUM]] deletes data files the table no longer references once they have been removed for longer than the retention, seven days by default. It never deletes log files and is not automatic in open-source Delta. Notice in the equations that a file removed minutes ago is not eligible, which is why the lab's dry run listed no data file. A shorter retention can break readers or streams still using old files, so the safety check refuses it.

handbook.markdown:
Look before deleting, and use the table's retention:

```sql
VACUUM inspections DRY RUN;   -- lists candidates, deletes nothing, commits nothing
VACUUM inspections;           -- only after the dry run and the owners' retention decision
```

**What the lab showed.** With every replaced file minutes old, `VACUUM ... DRY RUN` listed no Parquet file (the only path it printed was the `_change_data` directory entry itself). A request for `RETAIN 0 HOURS`, made only in DRY RUN mode, was refused before anything was listed:

```text
requirement failed: Are you sure you would like to vacuum files with such a low retention period?
```

Version 0 was still readable afterwards.

**Why the check exists.** The documentation recommends at least seven days because old snapshots and uncommitted files can still be in use by concurrent readers or writers: a VACUUM that removes them can make readers fail or, worse, corrupt the table. The interval must exceed the longest-running transaction and the longest lag of any stream reading the table. Keep the check on; never switch it off for a shared table.

**What a VACUUM removes.** Data files, including change files under `_change_data`, and time travel to any version whose files are gone. It does not remove log files, which checkpoint cleanup handles under `delta.logRetentionDuration` (30 days by default). **To keep more history**, raise `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` on the table (the documentation's example is 30 days) and accept the storage cost. Any change to a shared table's retention is a decision for its owners, recorded with the readers it affects.

beats.recap: A file is eligible only after removal plus the full retention; keep the safety check on and decide retention with the owners.

beats.title: Liquid clustering keeps layout keys you can change later
beats.outcome: Choose between partitioning, Z-ordering and liquid clustering for a filter pattern, and say what happens when the keys change.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delta-writes-clustering-concept|Liquid clustering]] declares clustering keys with CLUSTER BY; OPTIMIZE then clusters data incrementally, rewriting only what needs it. Keys can change with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY without rewriting existing files, and OPTIMIZE FULL reclusters everything. Notice in the comparison that clustering replaces partitioning and ZORDER instead of combining with them. In open-source Delta you choose the keys; Databricks can also choose them automatically.

handbook.markdown:
```sql
CREATE TABLE inspections (inspection_id STRING, plant STRING, inspected_on DATE, inspected INT)
USING delta CLUSTER BY (plant, inspected_on);

OPTIMIZE inspections;                  -- clusters new data incrementally
ALTER TABLE inspections CLUSTER BY (plant, inspection_id);   -- new keys; existing files not rewritten
OPTIMIZE inspections FULL;             -- reclusters all records (Delta 3.3 and above)
```

**Choosing keys.** Start from the filters queries actually use; up to four keys, each a column with collected statistics (by default the first 32 columns). If two candidate keys are correlated, one is enough. Converting a partitioned table: use the partition columns as keys; converting a Z-ordered table: use the ZORDER BY columns.

**Protocol cost.** The lab's clustered table showed `clustering` and `domainMetadata` in its features with writer version 7 and reader version 1: every writer must support both features, readers are unaffected, and the documentation says the protocol cannot be downgraded. `DESCRIBE DETAIL` reports `clusteringColumns`.

**Limits.** Changing keys affects later OPTIMIZE and writes only; old files keep their old layout until OPTIMIZE FULL. Liquid clustering is available in open-source Delta from 3.1 (as a preview flag in 3.1) with key changes from 3.2. **On Databricks**, automatic clustering lets the platform choose the keys for managed tables (keys set to AUTO); its requirements, including table type and predictive optimization, are read on the current Databricks page before relying on it.

beats.recap: Liquid clustering replaces partitions and Z-order with keys that OPTIMIZE applies incrementally and you can change.
beats.changeNote: Corrected the comparison table: changing a table's partitioning does not need a new table, because an overwrite with overwriteSchema can replace the partitioning by rewriting all data (Delta Lake's batch reads and writes documentation, delta-batch.md, at the v4.0.0 tag).

beats.title: Predictive optimization schedules maintenance on Databricks, not in open-source Delta
beats.outcome: Separate the open-source maintenance mechanisms from the Databricks-only service that schedules them, and state what to verify before relying on either.
beats.explanation: OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, liquid clustering and the change data feed are open-source Delta mechanisms you run yourself. [[dbxfe-delta-writes-predictive-concept|Predictive optimization]] is a Databricks service for Unity Catalog managed tables that decides when to run maintenance such as OPTIMIZE and VACUUM; it is enabled, disabled or inherited per catalog and schema. Notice in the comparison that automation changes who schedules the work, not what retention or clustering keys mean. Availability, defaults and billing are verified per account and region.

handbook.markdown:
Separate three layers when someone says 'Delta does maintenance for us':

| Layer | Open-source Delta 4.0 | Databricks |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | OPTIMIZE, ZORDER, VACUUM, CLUSTER BY, change data feed | the same commands, with runtime-specific details |
| Write-time help | auto compaction and optimized writes (3.1 and above) | platform defaults, read per runtime |
| Scheduler | none: you schedule jobs | predictive optimization for Unity Catalog managed tables |

The Databricks Terraform provider documents the switch at catalog and schema level, `enable_predictive_optimization` with the values `ENABLE`, `DISABLE` or `INHERIT`, and the same provider shows automatic clustering on a managed table by setting its clustering keys to `AUTO`. Databricks' own pages describe what the service runs and where it is available; the module's source records say which of those pages were confirmed in this build and which must be re-read.

**What to verify before relying on it.** The table is a Unity Catalog managed table; the effective setting at account, catalog and schema (an inherited flag can be off); the table's retention property, which still decides how much history stays readable; and region, defaults and billing on the current pages (check current pricing rather than estimating).

**What it does not change.** A MERGE still needs its guard, a snapshot delete still needs its scope, and a retention decision still needs its owners. Automation removes the scheduling chore, not the judgement recorded in the maintenance decision table.

beats.recap: The mechanisms are open source; predictive optimization is a Databricks scheduler for Unity Catalog managed tables.

beats.title: A maintenance decision names its effect on files, reads, compatibility and recovery
beats.outcome: Fill a maintenance decision table for a shared table and name the owners who must agree to each row.
beats.explanation: Every maintenance action touches four things: the files on disk, what current and old readers see, which clients can still read or write, and how far back you can recover. A [[dbxfe-delta-writes-decision-concept|maintenance decision record]] writes those four effects down before anything runs. Notice in the table that OPTIMIZE adds files and keeps history, VACUUM removes history, and enabling a feature changes compatibility, while none of them changes a row.

handbook.markdown:
A decision record is short and specific. For the Cinderline inspections table:

| Action | Files | Reads | Compatibility | Recovery | Agreed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OPTIMIZE nightly after the merge | adds one compacted file per run | same rows | unchanged | unchanged until VACUUM | platform team |
| VACUUM weekly at the 7-day default | deletes files removed over 7 days ago | current unchanged | unchanged | time travel limited to 7 days | table owner, dashboard and export owners |
| Enable change data feed | change files for later commits | change reads for the export | writer feature | changes readable from then on | table owner and every writer's owner |
| CLUSTER BY (plant, inspected_on) on a new table | rewritten by OPTIMIZE | same rows | clustering and domainMetadata | unchanged | table owner and main query owners |

**Evidence to collect first.** `DESCRIBE DETAIL` for the protocol and file count; `DESCRIBE HISTORY` for recent operations and their metrics; the longest-running reader and stream lag; a `VACUUM ... DRY RUN` listing; the client list with versions.

**What the record prevents.** Three failures it makes visible before they happen: a retention shortened to save storage that breaks a lagging stream, a feature enabled that locks out a partner's reader, a VACUUM run during a long export. The record names the owner of each risk, and it is the artefact the scenario asks for.

**Open-source or Databricks.** On Databricks, predictive optimization may run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for Unity Catalog managed tables; the record then states that the service is enabled, which retention it will honour, and who watches its history.

beats.recap: Write each maintenance action's effect on files, reads, compatibility and recovery, and who agreed, before it runs.

extensionCards.prompt: What does VACUUM LITE skip that the default VACUUM mode does?
extensionCards.answer: Listing the whole table directory: LITE finds removable files from the transaction log instead.
extensionCards.explanation: Open-source Delta 3.3 and above offers LITE mode, which is faster on large tables because it trusts the log to name files no longer referenced by any version within the retention. It cannot see files the table never referenced, such as leftovers from failed writes, which the default mode finds by listing the directory, and it fails with DELTA_CANNOT_VACUUM_LITE when the log entries it needs have been pruned. Neither mode relaxes the retention or the safety check.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Choosing a VACUUM mode for a large table depends on which files each mode can see and when LITE refuses.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can time travel fail inside 30 days even though nobody ran VACUUM?
extensionCards.answer: Old log entries are cleaned up at checkpoints, and a version needs every entry since its checkpoint.
extensionCards.explanation: delta.logRetentionDuration defaults to 30 days, and cleanup happens when checkpoints are written. The documentation's example: with log entries for versions 0 to 19 and a checkpoint at version 10, cleaning up the entry for version 0 makes versions 1 to 9 unreadable, because reconstructing them needs consecutive entries from a checkpoint. Keeping history longer therefore means planning the log retention as well as the file retention.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It explains a time-travel failure that has nothing to do with VACUUM and names the second retention to plan.

extensionCards.prompt: Why does repeating OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY cost again when plain OPTIMIZE does not?
extensionCards.answer: Z-ordering re-clusters all files of a partition on every run, while bin-packing skips already compacted files.
extensionCards.explanation: The documentation calls bin-packing idempotent and Z-ordering not idempotent: each ZORDER BY run builds a new clustering across the new and existing files of the partition, so its cost repeats on every schedule. Liquid clustering is incremental instead, rewriting only data that needs clustering, and it cannot be combined with ZORDER on the same table.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A maintenance job sized for plain OPTIMIZE can become expensive when someone adds ZORDER BY to it.

extensionCards.prompt: What happens to a stream reading a Delta table when a column is added?
extensionCards.answer: The stream stops at the schema change and must be restarted before it continues.
extensionCards.explanation: The open-source documentation states that updating a Delta table's schema terminates streams reading from it. A planned column addition therefore needs the stream owner's agreement and a restart plan, and a change-feed reader uses the latest version's schema. Renames and drops are not additive; done without rewriting data files they need column mapping, which brings further limits for change-feed reads.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It turns a harmless-looking ADD COLUMNS into a scheduled change for every streaming consumer of the table.

recap.title: Clauses decide rows; maintenance decides files and history
recap.markdown: **A MERGE changes rows only through the clauses you write**: matched rows update, unmatched source rows insert, and target rows the source omits change only through a delete-by-source clause, which belongs to complete snapshots and must carry their scope. De-duplicate before every merge and guard updates by revision. The change data feed records from the commit that enables it, enforcement refuses surprise columns, and evolution is a deliberate commit that may add table features. **Maintenance never changes a row**: OPTIMIZE rewrites files, VACUUM deletes history past a retention that its owners decide, and predictive optimization only schedules that work on Databricks. **Transfer challenge:** fill the decision table for a table whose change-feed consumer lags twelve days and whose supplier reads it with a client that does not support deletion vectors.

appliedTask.title: Plan the week's writes and maintenance for a changed delivery
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline adds a West plant. West sends a complete snapshot of its open lots every morning and North's incremental files keep occasional duplicate rows. A supplier's export reads the change data feed and can lag nine days; a monthly audit time-travels up to 14 days back. The team also wants liquid clustering on (plant, inspected_on) and asks whether to enable deletion vectors. Write the West merge, the North preparation and merge, the retention and VACUUM decision, and the clustering and deletion-vector decision, each with its effect on files, reads, compatibility and recovery.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: West: MERGE with WHEN MATCHED AND s.revision > t.revision THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.plant = 'West' THEN DELETE, after checking the snapshot's row count. North: keep the highest revision per key, send same-revision rows with different values to review, then merge with the guard and no delete clause. Retention: raise delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration above the longer of the nine-day lag and the 14-day audit, say 16 days, and plan the log retention to match; run a DRY RUN, then a scheduled VACUUM with the safety check on, agreed by the table, export and audit owners. Clustering: CLUSTER BY (plant, inspected_on) on an unpartitioned table, OPTIMIZE after the merges; it adds writer features, so confirm every writer's version. Deletion vectors: they are a reader feature, so defer them until the supplier confirms its reader supports them.
appliedTask.reasoning: Each decision follows one mechanism from the module: scope for snapshot deletes, guards for replays, retention from the longest consumer, and protocol features checked against every client before enabling them.
